title: Acme AI - Technical deep dive: priority routing, SLOs, and overload behavior
summary: Acme AI asked for a deep dive on Redwood’s new hot-route capacity protection (priority routing + tier-aware quotas) for /v1/chat/completions and embeddings. Team aligned on enterprise SLO targets (p95/p99 latency + availability), what happens under overload (admission control, backpressure, controlled shedding), and how 429s are classified (quota vs overload) with retry guidance. Acme’s main concerns were noisy-neighbor incidents, predictability during bursts, and auditability of throttling decisions. Redwood proposed a 2–3 week pilot in us-east with allowlisted enterprise keys, dashboards, and weekly SLO review; discussed optional Dedicated as a follow-on if they need stricter isolation.
topics: Acme workload + traffic shape (burstiness, token lengths, concurrency)
Protected routes and enterprise vs best-effort priority classes
Tier-aware rate limits vs quotas (windows, bursts) and headers
Overload behavior: admission control, queue depth signals, shedding order
Rollout plan (canary, allowlist, rollback) and pilot next steps
questions: Can we get deterministic explanation of why a request was throttled (quota vs overload vs per-route budget)?
What is the retry/backoff guidance for streaming vs non-streaming chat requests?
If the region is saturated, do you fail over to another region or model automatically, and can we disable fallback for quality reasons?
How are SLOs defined per route (chat vs embeddings) and how are alerts triggered?
Can we reserve a minimum capacity for our enterprise key on shared Hosted, or do we need Dedicated for that?
next_steps: Redwood to share draft pilot plan (protected routes, SLO targets, allowlisted keys, rollback criteria) by 2025-12-06.
Acme to send last 14 days traffic snapshot (RPS by route, p95 input/output tokens, burst peak, streaming mix) by 2025-12-09.
Redwood to provision enterprise-tier test project + API keys and enable hot-route protection flags in us-east for Acme allowlist by 2025-12-11.
Schedule 60-min pilot kickoff + dashboard walkthrough (SRE + Platform) week of 2025-12-15.
Redwood to send 429 reason code + header documentation and example client retry logic (incl. streaming) by 2025-12-06.
action_items: Liam O'Rourke - Email recap + propose pilot timeline and owners - Due 2025-12-06
Simran Kaur - Provide sample configs for per-route limits/quotas and recommended client retry/backoff - Due 2025-12-06
Rafael Mendes - Share dashboard links/queries and alert thresholds used for protected routes in canary - Due 2025-12-10
Miguel Santos - Export Acme traffic shape details (RPS, tokens, concurrency, burst peaks) - Due 2025-12-09
Daniel Cho - Confirm which routes are in-scope for pilot (chat, embeddings, rerank) and whether fallback is allowed - Due 2025-12-09
transcript:
Meeting: Acme AI - Technical deep dive: priority routing, SLOs, and overload behavior
Recorded: 2025-12-04 17:00:12 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke, Simran Kaur, Ravi Menon, Rafael Mendes, Nikhil Sharma
- Acme AI: Sarah Lang, Daniel Cho, Miguel Santos, Erin Wu

---

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, cool. We’re recording. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is to go deeper than the sales overview and get into the mechanics of priority routing, SLOs, and what happens when the fleet is under pressure. Sarah, Daniel, Miguel, Erin — anything you want to make sure we cover up front?

[00:22] Sarah Lang: Yeah. Our big thing is we’ve been burned by noisy neighbor problems. Like we buy “enterprise” and then a surge elsewhere causes our p99 to go to the moon. So, we want to understand, like, what you’re doing to prevent that. And what we can actually count on in terms of SLO.

[00:44] Daniel Cho: And I want specifics. Like do you rate limit by requests, tokens, concurrency, what are the 429 semantics, can we distinguish quota vs overload, all that.

[00:56] Miguel Santos: Also how do you surface this in metrics. If we get throttled, I need to know why without opening a ticket.

[01:04] Liam O'Rourke: Yep. Makes sense. I’m gonna let Ravi walk through the architecture, Simran will cover the customer-facing contract, and Rafael will speak to SLOs and what we alert on. Nikhil is here as product lead for Hosted API tier semantics.

[01:21] Nikhil Sharma: Hey everyone.

[01:23] Ravi Menon: Hi.

[01:24] Simran Kaur: Hi.

[01:25] Rafael Mendes: Hey.

[01:27] Liam O'Rourke: Quick framing: this initiative internally is “hot-route capacity protection.” It’s for the high-traffic, high-SLA routes like /v1/chat/completions, embeddings, rerank. The idea is to prevent fleet-wide degradation when one route or one customer workload shape is overwhelming shared GPU pools.

[01:49] Sarah Lang: Great.

[01:51] Ravi Menon: I’ll start with the enforcement points because that’s usually the confusing part. There’s three places you can do it: API gateway, routing layer, and runtime scheduler. We do a bit in all three, but the primary “policy decision” is evaluated once, early, and then used downstream.

[02:10] Daniel Cho: So the gateway is actually making admission decisions?

[02:13] Ravi Menon: For some things, yes. Like static per-tier rate limits and quota checks: request-based, windowed, that is cheap and deterministic. For overload, it’s not purely gateway because you need fleet signals like queue depth, scheduler lag. Those signals feed into routing/admission.

[02:30] Miguel Santos: What are the signals exactly? GPU utilization is noisy.

[02:33] Ravi Menon: Right. We learned that. Primary is queue depth at the runtime and a scheduler lag metric. GPU saturation alone is a trailing indicator. So the routing layer watches queue depth by pool and will gate best-effort traffic first.

[02:49] Rafael Mendes: And just to be clear, “gate” means: we return 429 with consistent reason codes, versus letting requests enter queues and then time out into 5xx.

[03:01] Sarah Lang: That’s good. We’d rather get a fast 429 than a 90 second hang.

[03:06] Simran Kaur: Same. The customer experience is “predictable failure.” And for enterprise routes, we try to avoid failing you unless we’ve exhausted best-effort budgets.

[03:16] Daniel Cho: Okay, but what does that mean, “budgets”? Like a reserved slice?

[03:20] Simran Kaur: Think of it as per-route and per-priority class admission budgets. It’s not quite hard reservation like dedicated GPUs, but it’s a controlled policy: enterprise class has higher priority, and there’s a minimum share protected under overload conditions.

[03:37] Daniel Cho: So still shared pool.

[03:39] Liam O'Rourke: Correct on Hosted. Dedicated is the “hard isolation” product. But this project is specifically to make Hosted and Dedicated behave better under overload.

[03:49] Erin Wu: We’re probably starting with Hosted for the pilot. Dedicated might be phase 2.

[03:53] Nikhil Sharma: And we can talk about what triggers the “you should be on Dedicated” conversation. Usually it’s sustained throughput requirements plus strict data isolation requirements.

[04:04] Rafael Mendes: Maybe it’s helpful if I outline the SLO model. For protected enterprise routes, we define route-specific SLO targets: availability and latency, typically p95 and p99, measured at the edge.

[04:17] Sarah Lang: What kind of numbers are we talking?

[04:20] Rafael Mendes: Depends on model and region. For chat, with streaming, we focus on time-to-first-token and then tokens/sec. For non-streaming, we look at end-to-end latency. We don’t want to commit on this call to exact milliseconds without your traffic shape. But we can set targets in the pilot, and then we’ll validate.

[04:39] Daniel Cho: We’re mostly streaming, but not always. We do some batch embeddings as well.

[04:44] Simran Kaur: For embeddings, it’s more straightforward. For chat, we’ll separate TTFT from total.

[04:51] Miguel Santos: How do you map overload into SLO? Like if you 429 us, is that counted as an error?

[04:57] Rafael Mendes: Great question. For enterprise tier, quota-based 429 is kind of “expected” if you exceed your purchased quota; overload-based 429 is the protection mechanism, and we measure it explicitly. In SLO terms, overload-based shedding is still a failed request. The whole point is we shed best-effort first so enterprise sees less of it.

[05:16] Sarah Lang: And you alert on that?

[05:18] Rafael Mendes: Yes, but we try not to page on expected best-effort shedding because that creates paging storms. For enterprise routes we page on sustained SLO burn or if enterprise shed rate crosses threshold for N minutes.

[05:34] Daniel Cho: Can we get those metrics in our side? Like headers or response fields.

[05:38] Simran Kaur: There are two layers. (1) Response headers: we include rate-limit headers and also a “reason code” header for 429. (2) In the console we expose aggregated metrics by route and tier; for the pilot we’ll give you access to that view, and we can also export via API.

[05:56] Miguel Santos: What’s the exact reason code? This is important.

[06:00] Simran Kaur: So, today the schema is: a 429 with a structured error body and a header. You’ll see something like “quota_exceeded” versus “overload_protection” (names may differ slightly in docs). There’s also a field indicating whether it was per-minute rate limit vs per-day quota window.

[06:19] Daniel Cho: Are these stable? Like if I code against them, is that safe.

[06:22] Nikhil Sharma: We treat them as part of the API contract. We’ll document them; we’re not going to randomly change strings without versioning.

[06:31] Sarah Lang: And what’s the guidance? Exponential backoff, jitter.

[06:35] Simran Kaur: Yes. And importantly, for overload-based 429, we want a slightly more aggressive backoff. The response includes a Retry-After value when we can estimate a safe retry window.

[06:48] Daniel Cho: “When we can” meaning sometimes it’s blank.

[06:51] Simran Kaur: Sometimes. For quota windows, Retry-After is clear. For overload, it’s derived from queue depth and smoothing, so we provide it when it’s reliable.

[07:02] Miguel Santos: For streaming: what happens if it starts streaming and then you shed mid-stream?

[07:07] Ravi Menon: Good one. We avoid that as much as possible. The admission control should happen before we start the stream. But there are failure modes where capacity collapses mid-flight. In that case we send a consistent termination with an error code, not just a TCP hang.

[07:23] Daniel Cho: Like an SSE “error” event?

[07:25] Ravi Menon: Exactly. Or the equivalent depending on SDK. And we tag it so you can distinguish “model error” vs “shedding.”

[07:34] Sarah Lang: Okay. That’s reassuring.

[07:36] Liam O'Rourke: Maybe we should get concrete on your workload so we can map to SLO and protections. Daniel, can you give a quick rundown: routes, typical tokens, bursts.

[07:46] Daniel Cho: Sure. We do /v1/chat/completions. Average prompt maybe 1.2k tokens, outputs 200-400. But we have long-tail prompts like 8k input if someone uploads a big context. Concurrency: baseline 200 rps, spikes to 800 rps during product launches. And then embeddings: we do batch jobs, like 10k docs at a time but we can throttle that.

[08:10] Erin Wu: Those batch jobs can be scheduled off-peak.

[08:12] Miguel Santos: The scary part is the spike. That’s user-driven.

[08:15] Ravi Menon: Got it. The long prompts are relevant because they hold KV cache longer and can blow up queue depth. One of our protections is to incorporate request “cost” signals in admission policies. It’s not perfect token-based accounting in the critical path, but we can classify request sizes.

[08:33] Daniel Cho: So you’re not doing per-token rate limiting at the gateway.

[08:36] Ravi Menon: Not on the hot path. We do request-based limits plus workload-shape aware routing. Full fairness scheduler rewrite is not in scope right now.

[08:47] Daniel Cho: Okay.

[08:48] Sarah Lang: But does that mean someone can send giant prompts and hog resources.

[08:53] Rafael Mendes: This is why we’re doing the per-route per-tier budgets. For enterprise chat routes, you get protected budgets. For best-effort, we shed earlier. Additionally we can set guardrails on max input tokens by tier if needed.

[09:10] Miguel Santos: Are those guardrails configurable per customer.

[09:12] Simran Kaur: We can set per-project overrides. But we try to keep it standardized to avoid surprise.

[09:18] Liam O'Rourke: For the pilot, we’ll start with defaults and then we can tune based on your traffic snapshot.

[09:25] Daniel Cho: What about priority classes. Is it just enterprise vs best-effort?

[09:29] Nikhil Sharma: For now, yes: enterprise and best-effort are the primary externally-visible tiers. Internally we also have system/internal traffic and background jobs, but customer-facing is those.

[09:41] Daniel Cho: Can we get a “super enterprise” class for certain keys.

[09:44] Liam O'Rourke: That becomes a contract / exception discussion. We do have allowlists and per-account policies for specific enterprise needs, but we want to be careful.

[09:54] Sarah Lang: We have two products. One is like mission-critical, the other is not.

[09:58] Simran Kaur: In that case we can split by project or API key and apply different per-route budgets.

[10:05] Miguel Santos: As long as it’s auditable.

[10:07] Ravi Menon: Auditability is a big requirement. Policy decisions are logged deterministically (like a decision record) with the inputs: route group, tier, current overload signal state, and the outcome.

[10:22] Miguel Santos: Is that something we can see.

[10:25] Ravi Menon: Not directly today for customers, but for pilot we can share extracts in weekly reviews. Internally we have a debug endpoint for on-call. For customer exposure, we’re building “explain” views in console.

[10:38] Daniel Cho: So if we open a ticket you can say “it was overload, queue depth high, you were best-effort” etc.

[10:43] Ravi Menon: Exactly. And for you, since you’ll be enterprise tier in pilot, the question will be: did enterprise shed happen, and if yes, what else was going on in region.

[10:55] Sarah Lang: Let’s talk about regional failover. If us-east is hot, do you send to us-west.

[11:00] Ravi Menon: By default, we do not silently fail you across regions for enterprise chat without your approval because of data residency and potential latency changes. We can configure fallback policies per route.

[11:13] Daniel Cho: We don’t want silent model fallback either. Quality changes.

[11:16] Simran Kaur: Yup. For protected enterprise routes, fallback is opt-in. You can choose strict admission control only, meaning we’d rather 429 than change model.

[11:27] Sarah Lang: I prefer that.

[11:29] Rafael Mendes: Operationally, strict mode is easier for SLO math, too.

[11:34] Erin Wu: For embeddings, I don’t care as much. For chat, yes strict.

[11:38] Simran Kaur: We can set: embeddings route group allows fallback to compatible model variant if capacity constrained; chat stays strict.

[11:49] Daniel Cho: Compatible variant like a different quantization.

[11:52] Ravi Menon: Sometimes. Or a different GPU pool. But again, only if you allow.

[11:59] Liam O'Rourke: Sarah, can you share your SLO expectations? Like what’s acceptable.

[12:04] Sarah Lang: For chat, availability 99.9 on the API. Latency, we measure user-perceived, but basically we want TTFT under 1.5 seconds at p95. p99, maybe under 4 seconds. If it degrades, we want it to degrade gracefully and predictably, not random timeouts.

[12:25] Rafael Mendes: That’s helpful. We’ll sanity check with your token distribution; TTFT depends a lot on prompt length and model. But in terms of protection mechanisms, the goal is exactly that: enterprise stays stable while best-effort gets throttled earlier.

[12:41] Miguel Santos: Can you explain the “throttled earlier” part. Like do you preempt best-effort first.

[12:46] Ravi Menon: Yes. Under overload signal, the admission controller reduces best-effort budget first, potentially to near zero, while preserving enterprise budgets. That keeps queues short for enterprise.

[12:59] Daniel Cho: So you’re not literally preempting running requests.

[13:02] Ravi Menon: Not preempting GPU kernels mid-flight, no. It’s admission control, not preemption.

[13:09] Daniel Cho: Good.

[13:10] Sarah Lang: And if enterprise load itself is too high.

[13:14] Rafael Mendes: Then we’ll shed enterprise too, but with clear signals and alerts. This is where Dedicated might be needed if your “enterprise baseline” is basically the whole pool.

[13:28] Liam O'Rourke: The pilot will help us see where you land.

[13:31] Erin Wu: What about quotas. We need to make sure our batch jobs don’t eat the quota.

[13:36] Simran Kaur: Quotas can be defined per route group. So embeddings batch could have a separate daily quota bucket than interactive chat.

[13:47] Erin Wu: That’s what we want.

[13:49] Daniel Cho: Can you show an example of the headers.

[13:52] Simran Kaur: Yeah. It’s like:
- X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset
- And for 429, a reason header like X-Redwood-Error-Reason: quota_exceeded or overload_protection
- Plus Retry-After in seconds when applicable.

[14:12] Miguel Santos: The names might change slightly though.

[14:14] Simran Kaur: We’ll send the exact doc after this. I’m paraphrasing.

[14:18] Sarah Lang: Okay.

[14:20] Liam O'Rourke: Maybe we talk about rollout and commitments. This is newly GA’d protection in our us-east canary and rolling to more regions. For your pilot we can enable it on an allowlist in us-east.

[14:35] Daniel Cho: Is it safe? Like are there known issues.

[14:38] Rafael Mendes: We had a metric cardinality issue early on (too many tags). That’s fixed. Functionally, the risk is mostly mis-tuned thresholds causing extra 429s. That’s why we do a pilot with tight monitoring.

[14:54] Miguel Santos: And can you roll it back quickly.

[14:56] Ravi Menon: Yes. Feature flags, region-by-region, and allowlist per account. Rollback is basically flipping a flag and reverting to previous routing behavior.

[15:08] Sarah Lang: What does the pilot look like.

[15:10] Liam O'Rourke: Proposal: 2–3 weeks. Week 1 we baseline your performance with protection on but conservative thresholds. Week 2 we run a controlled overload simulation (not on your production traffic unless you want), see if enterprise stays stable while best-effort is shed. Week 3 we finalize SLO targets, dashboards, and a go/no-go for broader rollout or Dedicated.

[15:34] Daniel Cho: Are we the only customer in that pool.

[15:36] Liam O'Rourke: No, Hosted is shared. But you’ll be in enterprise priority class.

[15:42] Daniel Cho: That’s the whole point.

[15:43] Sarah Lang: Yeah.

[15:45] Ravi Menon: To add: the “hot routes” are protected at the route group level. So /v1/chat/completions is a protected route group. That reduces the chance that, say, some random less-important endpoint causes an issue. The protection is focused on the hotspots.

[16:04] Erin Wu: What about embeddings. That’s a hot route too.

[16:08] Ravi Menon: Yes. Embeddings and rerank are also in the protected set.

[16:13] Miguel Santos: If a customer spams embeddings, do they hurt chat.

[16:17] Ravi Menon: It depends on pool configuration, but generally yes, it can. Part of the policy is per-route budgets so chat enterprise doesn’t get drowned by embeddings best-effort.

[16:30] Daniel Cho: So budgets are per route group AND tier.

[16:33] Ravi Menon: Exactly.

[16:35] Sarah Lang: Can you define “hot route.” Is that just you deciding.

[16:38] Nikhil Sharma: We maintain an internal inventory based on traffic and SLA impact. Customers can request a route be treated as protected, but usually it’s the core ones.

[16:49] Daniel Cho: If we use a new endpoint in the future, we’d want the same protection.

[16:53] Nikhil Sharma: Yep. We’d evaluate it and likely add it.

[16:58] Miguel Santos: On observability: do you have per-route, per-tier graphs.

[17:02] Rafael Mendes: Yes. At a minimum: request rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx, 429 broken down by reason, and shed rate. Also queue depth and scheduler lag at the backend. We annotate when protection triggers.

[17:18] Miguel Santos: Great. Can we integrate with Datadog.

[17:21] Rafael Mendes: We can export metrics via our telemetry API. For the pilot we can start with console dashboards and we’ll give you the data.

[17:30] Daniel Cho: If we see 429 overload, what should the client do. Retry right away? Queue.

[17:36] Simran Kaur: We recommend backoff with jitter. For interactive requests, maybe 200-500ms initial with exponential. For batch embeddings, you can do longer backoff and respect Retry-After.

[17:51] Daniel Cho: We already have a retry loop but we need to avoid thundering herd.

[17:54] Simran Kaur: Exactly. We’ll send a reference snippet.

[17:59] Sarah Lang: What about SLA. Will you put this in writing.

[18:03] Liam O'Rourke: For a pilot, we typically do a pilot addendum with target SLOs and reporting, but not a full SLA until contract stage. That said, the whole reason we built this is to support SLA-backed enterprise deals.

[18:20] Sarah Lang: Okay.

[18:21] Daniel Cho: I want to push on determinism. If you’re doing routing decisions based on queue depth, that can be kind of fuzzy.

[18:29] Ravi Menon: Totally. Deterministic doesn’t mean “never changes”; it means: given the signals and the policy config at time T, the decision is explainable. We record the threshold state and the policy evaluation outcome.

[18:44] Miguel Santos: So you log what threshold was crossed.

[18:46] Ravi Menon: Yes. Like “overload_state=active, signal=queue_depth, pool=xyz, tier=best_effort, decision=shed.” That kind of thing.

[18:57] Daniel Cho: And for enterprise, decision=admit.

[18:59] Ravi Menon: Usually. Unless enterprise also exceeds its budget.

[19:04] Sarah Lang: How do you set enterprise budget.

[19:07] Nikhil Sharma: Defaults are based on tiering and historical usage. For pilot we tune with you. There’s also a commercial side: if you need a bigger guaranteed share, that maps to your commit.

[19:20] Sarah Lang: Okay.

[19:22] Erin Wu: What about cost. If we get 429’d less, we’ll spend more.

[19:27] Liam O'Rourke: Potentially, but it’s more about predictability. You can still cap with quotas. And you can separate batch to a different quota.

[19:37] Daniel Cho: We might want per-minute caps for batch to not interfere.

[19:41] Simran Kaur: That’s straightforward. Rate limits per route group.

[19:47] Miguel Santos: How does this compare to like Bedrock provisioned throughput.

[19:51] Liam O'Rourke: Provisioned throughput is closer to our Dedicated. Hosted enterprise is more like priority lanes with protection and SLO, but shared infra. If you want “you own this slice,” dedicated is the analog.

[20:08] Sarah Lang: We’re not ready for dedicated cost maybe.

[20:10] Liam O'Rourke: Understood. Pilot on Hosted first.

[20:13] Daniel Cho: Mentioned competitors—Together, Anyscale—some of them do token-based rate limiting.

[20:19] Ravi Menon: Yes, and it’s not that token-based is bad. It’s the overhead and correctness tradeoffs at high QPS. We can still incorporate request cost classes without full per-token enforcement at the gateway.

[20:35] Daniel Cho: Okay.

[20:36] Sarah Lang: I’d like to understand the “controlled shedding” order. Like do you drop new requests or can you cancel old ones.

[20:43] Rafael Mendes: It’s primarily dropping new admissions when overload state is active. We also have backpressure to slow acceptance. Canceling in-flight is not the primary strategy.

[20:55] Sarah Lang: That’s fine.

[20:57] Miguel Santos: How quickly does overload state clear.

[21:00] Ravi Menon: There’s hysteresis to avoid flapping. For example, queue depth needs to remain below threshold for some window.

[21:10] Daniel Cho: Otherwise clients will oscillate.

[21:12] Ravi Menon: Exactly.

[21:14] Simran Kaur: And for the API contract, you’ll see fewer “random” 5xx timeouts because we’d rather reject early.

[21:24] Erin Wu: That’s our main pain. Timeouts cause retries and amplify.

[21:28] Rafael Mendes: Cascade failures, yep.

[21:31] Sarah Lang: Can you talk about the last incident that motivated this. Not details, just pattern.

[21:36] Rafael Mendes: High-level: one route had a sudden burst with long prompts, queue depth rose, latency p99 spiked, customers retried, and it cascaded into fleet-wide saturation. Without admission control, the system accepted too much and fell over. With the new system, best-effort would have been shed earlier and the “blast radius” would be contained.

[22:00] Sarah Lang: Got it.

[22:02] Daniel Cho: What about per-customer isolation. If another enterprise customer spikes, do they hurt us.

[22:08] Ravi Menon: Within enterprise class, we still have per-account quotas and rate limits. There’s not full fairness scheduling across enterprise tenants, but the tier-aware quotas help. If you want strict isolation, again Dedicated.

[22:22] Sarah Lang: Okay. So enterprise Hosted is “protected but not isolated.”

[22:27] Liam O'Rourke: That’s a fair summary.

[22:29] Miguel Santos: During the pilot, can you show us your internal dashboards.

[22:33] Rafael Mendes: We can share a curated view: queue depth, shed rates, tier breakdown. Some internal panels have sensitive multi-tenant details, but we can provide what you need.

[22:46] Daniel Cho: Okay.

[22:48] Simran Kaur: Also, we can set up a weekly review where we go through 429 rates by reason. If we see overload-based 429 for enterprise, that’s a red flag.

[23:00] Sarah Lang: Great.

[23:02] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s talk about what you need from us to start. Miguel, you mentioned you want to know “why” without a ticket. The reason codes plus dashboards should help. Are you okay with that for pilot.

[23:16] Miguel Santos: If reason codes are stable, and we get a dashboard, yes. Longer term we’d like an API.

[23:23] Simran Kaur: Understood.

[23:25] Daniel Cho: Also we need guidance for client backoff. Especially for streaming.

[23:30] Simran Kaur: We’ll send it.

[23:32] Erin Wu: On quotas: can we set daily caps and also per-minute. Like two layers.

[23:37] Nikhil Sharma: Yes. Rate limit (per minute) plus quota (per day/month). We can do both per route group.

[23:47] Erin Wu: Great.

[23:49] Sarah Lang: What is your rollout commitment. Like if we do pilot and it works, can we get it in two regions.

[23:56] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, after pilot we can expand. It’s feature-flagged and rolling out region by region. us-east is easiest, then eu-west, us-west depending on your needs.

[24:11] Sarah Lang: Data residency. We need US only.

[24:14] Liam O'Rourke: Then us-east/us-west.

[24:16] Daniel Cho: For latency we prefer east.

[24:18] Miguel Santos: But we need DR.

[24:20] Ravi Menon: DR can be strict failover: only if region is unavailable, not for capacity. That’s a policy choice.

[24:29] Daniel Cho: That’s good.

[24:31] Sarah Lang: Ok.

[24:33] Liam O'Rourke: Switching gears: your current provider. Are you on OpenAI or self-hosted.

[24:38] Sarah Lang: Mix. We have some OpenAI, and we self-host vLLM for a smaller model. OpenAI has reliability but cost is high. Self-host is cost-effective but we get paged for everything.

[24:52] Daniel Cho: And OpenAI sometimes rate limits us unpredictably.

[24:55] Simran Kaur: Right. We’re trying to make 429 semantics predictable and documented.

[25:02] Miguel Santos: We’re fine with 429s if we can plan for them.

[25:06] Rafael Mendes: Exactly.

[25:08] Daniel Cho: Can we talk about token/sec. If under pressure, does the system slow down tokens per second.

[25:15] Ravi Menon: Under pressure, tokens/sec can degrade if queues form. The protection aims to keep queues low for enterprise. But if enterprise load itself saturates, you could see tokens/sec drop. That’s why budgets exist.

[25:29] Daniel Cho: Makes sense.

[25:31] Sarah Lang: This all sounds good, but we need to see it. We want evidence.

[25:35] Liam O'Rourke: 100%. Pilot + load test + dashboards.

[25:39] Rafael Mendes: We can also do a game-day style test where we inject load on best-effort and verify enterprise SLO stability.

[25:49] Miguel Santos: Is that safe in a shared system.

[25:52] Rafael Mendes: We do it carefully and can constrain to a specific pool / sandbox. For pilot, we can do it in a dedicated test project first.

[26:04] Erin Wu: We have staging traffic we can replay.

[26:07] Simran Kaur: Perfect.

[26:09] Daniel Cho: What about “rerank”. We might use it later.

[26:12] Nikhil Sharma: That’s in protected set. If you adopt, we can extend policies.
